Every number in this report is one of about a dozen kinds. This section defines each
one once, says what it assumes, and says how it fails. It is written to be skimmed on
first read and returned to when a specific figure is in question.

## Two units of measurement, and why both appear

**cp10k — counts per 10,000.** A transcript count divided by the total counts in the
same object, times 10,000. It removes differences in sequencing depth, which on this
platform vary by more than tenfold between cells and between fields of view.

<div class="verdict-no">
**`cp10k` means two different things in this project and they are not comparable.**
Step 11 and every bin- or region-level table use the *pooled* share: all counts in the
region are summed, then divided by the region's summed total. Step 10's per-gene tables
use the *mean of per-cell* shares. The pooled version weights a region's deep cells more
heavily; the per-cell mean weights every cell equally and is dominated by shallow cells.
A pooled value and a per-cell-mean value for the same gene in the same tissue can differ
by severalfold. This report states which is in use at each table.
</div>

**The compositional trap.** cp10k is a *share* of a fixed total, so shares must sum to
one. If a handful of genes rise steeply in a region, every other gene's share falls
even when its absolute transcription is unchanged. The effect is largest for genes that
are already abundant, because they have the most share to lose. This is not a subtle
correction: in this data it manufactures apparent *depression* of top-abundance genes in
exactly the regions where the disease programme is most active. Any single-gene cp10k
change, in either direction, has this as a live alternative explanation.

**Detection rate** — the fraction of cells in a region with at least one count of the
gene — is the second unit, used because it is not compositional. A cell either has the
transcript or it does not, and one gene rising does not lower another gene's detection.
Its weakness is the mirror image: detection saturates. Once a gene is found in most
cells, a real increase in transcription cannot show up as an increase in detection.

**The concordance gate.** Because each unit fails where the other is sound, no
single-gene result in this project is reported on one of them alone. A gene is called
differential only if the cp10k change and the detection-rate change point the *same
way*, and the detection-rate change is itself non-trivial:

> `sign(log2FC_cp10k) == sign(log2FC_detection)`  **and**  `|log2FC_detection| > 0.3`

The 0.3 threshold is about a 23% relative change in the fraction of cells positive.
Genes that pass significance on cp10k but fail concordance are retained in the output
tables, flagged, and not discussed as findings — they are the population most likely to
be compositional artifact. This gate is deliberately conservative and will discard some
true positives, particularly for abundant genes near detection saturation.

## Calling a single cell positive for a sparse gene

Several genes central to this report — *PDCD1*, *CD274*, *PDCD1LG2* — are detected in
only a few percent of cells. At that level the threshold for "positive" is not a
formality; it decides the answer.

The panel carries **negative-control probes** with no biological target. Their count
distribution is the platform's false-positive floor, measured on the same cells in the
same run. Calibrating against it (`negprobe_verdict.csv`):

- at **≥ 1 count**, *CD274* is 2.7× the mean blank probe and *PDCD1* 2.9× — near enough
  to the floor that a substantial share of "positive" cells are noise;
- at **≥ 2 counts**, the blank rate collapses to 0.05% and the same genes sit 25–31×
  above it. Every panel gene tested clears 10× specificity at this threshold.

**≥ 2 counts is therefore the per-cell positivity definition throughout.** The cost is
sensitivity: roughly 1–2% of cells are positive for the checkpoint genes, a few thousand
per sample. Consequences that follow from this and are stated wherever they bite: a null
per-cell result is a **floor result**, not evidence of absence; and the positive cells
are, by construction, enriched for deep cells.

<div class="verdict-mid">
**Sequencing depth predicts positivity for every sparse gene, including certainties.**
Depth discriminates positive from negative cells at AUC 0.64–0.76 for *every* gene
tested — including *IGKC* (0.693 / 0.733), *CD3E* (0.695 / 0.649) and *CD68* (0.731 /
0.671), which are unambiguously present. *PDCD1* (0.711) and *CD274* (0.699) are
indistinguishable from those. An AUC near 0.70 against depth is therefore a property of
any sparse count call on this platform and **not** a signature of a spurious gene. What
follows is not that the calls are unreliable but that **depth must be controlled in every
per-cell positivity comparison** — which is done here by stratification, below.
</div>

## The unit of a p-value

This is the single most consequential methodological choice in the project.

A field of view holds thousands of cells that share a section, a staining reaction, a
depth profile and a local tissue architecture. They are not independent observations of
the disease. Treating 400,000 cells as 400,000 samples produces p-values below 10<sup>-300</sup>
for effects that do not reproduce, because the test is measuring the certainty of a
*local* mean, not whether the biology differs. Step 11 lost a Tfh result to exactly this
error and it is the reason for the rule.

**In this project, the unit of every p-value is a spatial region — a 100 µm bin, a
neighbourhood, or a field of view — never a cell.** Counts are summed within each region
first (a *pseudobulk*), the region becomes one observation, and the test is run across
regions. Sample sizes in these tables are therefore in the tens to hundreds, and the
p-values are correspondingly modest. That is the honest scale of the evidence at n = 1.

**FOV collapse as a second, stricter reading.** Bins within one field of view still share
that field's technical batch. Where a result matters it is recomputed with the field of
view as the unit — a coarser and more conservative test, with fewer observations. Results
described as "surviving FOV collapse" passed both. Results significant at bin level but
not at FOV level are reported as bin-level only and are the weaker class of evidence.

## The tests

**Mann–Whitney U** (Wilcoxon rank-sum) compares two groups of regions on one gene. It
asks whether a randomly chosen region from group A tends to rank above one from group B.
It is used because it assumes nothing about the shape of the distribution — region-level
cp10k values are skewed and heavy-tailed, and a t-test's normality assumption is not met.
What it does assume is that the regions within a group are exchangeable, which is what
the unit rule above is protecting. It reports a shift in ranks, so a significant result
means "systematically higher", not "higher by X".

**Fold changes are reported alongside every p-value and are the quantity to read for
magnitude.** A Mann–Whitney p-value carries no effect size at all; a gene can be highly
significant on a small, uninteresting shift if the regions are consistent.

**Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (`q`).** Testing ~6,000 genes at p < 0.05 yields ~300 false
positives by construction. BH rescales p-values so that `q < 0.05` means *of the genes
called significant, about 5% are expected to be false* — a statement about the called set,
not about any single gene. It is applied within each contrast separately, so q-values are
not comparable across contrasts. BH assumes tests are independent or positively
correlated; co-expressed genes satisfy the latter well enough for the guarantee to hold
approximately, and it is the standard choice in this setting.

**Permutation nulls.** Where the question is spatial — is this set of bins clustered
rather than scattered, are these two cell types adjacent more often than expected — there
is no closed-form null. Instead labels are shuffled many times *within matched strata*
(density deciles, lineage) and the observed statistic is compared to the resulting
distribution. Shuffling within strata is the essential detail: an unstratified shuffle
would test the trivial hypothesis that cells are non-uniformly distributed in tissue,
which they obviously are, and would return significance for everything. The p-value is
the share of permutations at least as extreme as the observation, so its resolution is
bounded by the number of permutations — a reported *p* = 0.001 on 1,000 permutations means
"nothing this extreme occurred", not a precise value.

**Cluster bootstrap.** Confidence intervals on per-cell models are obtained by resampling
*fields of view with replacement*, refitting, and taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
of the resulting estimates. Resampling FOVs rather than cells is what propagates the
within-field correlation into the interval. A bootstrap that resampled cells (or bins)
would produce intervals far too narrow — this happened in an earlier version of the
cross-sample analysis, where a bin-resampling bootstrap drove ~900 genes to the p-value
floor simultaneously, which was the signal that the resampling unit was wrong.

**Mixed model as a cross-check, not as the primary fit.** Where a per-cell model matters,
the cluster-bootstrap estimate is refitted as a generalised linear mixed model with a
**random intercept per field of view** (`lme4::glmer`), which handles the same within-field
correlation by a different mechanism: the bootstrap makes no assumption about how fields
differ, while the mixed model assumes their intercepts are drawn from a normal distribution
and shrinks small fields toward the overall mean. Because the two rest on different
assumptions, agreement between them is informative and disagreement localises the problem.
Where they part company it is in the expected direction -- the contrast with the fewest
fields of view is the one the mixed model shrinks most. The bootstrap is reported as the
primary estimate because its assumptions are the weaker of the two.

**Spearman's ρ** is used for the gradient analyses (expression against a continuous field
level or a distance). It correlates *ranks*, so it detects any monotone relationship and
is not distorted by the long right tail of chemokine values. It will not detect a
non-monotone one — a signal that rises then falls with distance appears as ρ ≈ 0.

## Controlling depth and composition

**Depth-decile stratification.** In the per-cell binomial models, cells are cut into
deciles of total counts and the decile is entered as a covariate. The comparison is then
made *within* depth strata and pooled, so a region cannot appear positive merely because
its cells were sequenced more deeply. A necessary precondition is checked and reported
first: if the two regions' depth distributions do not overlap across enough deciles, the
region effect and the depth effect are not separately identifiable and no estimate is
issued for that contrast rather than a misleading one.

**Odds ratios.** The per-cell models are binomial (logistic) regressions of positivity,
so their effect size is an odds ratio: OR = 2 means the odds of a cell being positive are
doubled in the first region relative to the second, holding depth stratum constant. For
outcomes as rare as these (1–3%) an odds ratio is close to a risk ratio, so "roughly
twice as likely to be positive" is a fair reading. Intervals are the FOV cluster
bootstrap above. An interval that includes 1 is not evidence of no effect — with a few
hundred positive cells the intervals are wide, and the width is the result.

**Composition standardisation and matching.** Two regions with the same cell types in
different proportions will differ on almost every gene for that reason alone. Two devices
address it. Where possible the comparison is made **within a cell type**, which cannot be
moved by how many cells of that type are present. Where a region-level comparison is
needed, regions are **matched** on cell count, median depth, median area and B-cell share,
and the achieved balance is reported as a **standardised mean difference** — the group
difference in units of pooled SD. Below 0.1 is conventionally good balance; the
pre-matching values in this project reach 4.6–6.1, which is itself the central
negative finding of the cross-sample comparison rather than a nuisance to be fixed.

## Module scores, and the ceiling on them

Single genes at 1–3% detection are near-unusable per cell. Summing several genes that
mark the same biology raises detection: if each gene is detected independently with
probability *p*, the chance that at least one of *k* is detected is `1 - (1-p)^k`. At
*p* ≈ 0.05, five genes give ~23% and fifteen give ~54%. **The number of genes therefore
sets a hard ceiling on what a module can recover**, and modules built from few genes
cannot be rescued by any amount of statistics. Where a module remains under-detected this
is stated as a bound, with the arithmetic.

Two cautions applied throughout. A module is only as specific as its worst gene: an
IFN-γ-response module initially built here was dominated by *B2M*, *CD74* and *HLA-DRA*,
which report constitutive MHC expression rather than interferon signalling, and removing
them cut the effect from +0.623 to +0.219. And a module scored on the cells that defined
it is circular — so every module result is reported twice, with and without the defining
genes and cells, and **only the second is treated as evidence**.

## Power bounds

Where a comparison returns nothing, the report gives a **power bound**: the smallest
effect that would have been detected at 80% power given the observed positivity rate and
number of regions. This converts an uninformative "not significant" into a bounded
statement — *an effect larger than this would probably have been seen; anything smaller
would not have been*. Read it as the resolution limit of the measurement. A null result
with a bound of 2× is meaningful; a null with a bound of 10× says almost nothing.

## Difference-in-differences, and what it assumes

To ask whether FL behaves differently *next to a Hodgkin field*, the natural construction
is to take each sample's internal contrast (disease region versus its own reference) and
subtract one from the other. A technical offset affecting one whole sample cancels.

**It cancels only if the offset is the same in the reference region as in the disease
region** — that is, no sample × region interaction other than the biology of interest.
That assumption is not testable with one patient. Where it is checkable it is checked: if
the two samples' *reference* regions do not differ on the gene in question, the offset is
bounded and the subtraction is credible; if they differ substantially, the raw
cross-sample number is uninterpretable and the subtraction is the only honest version of
it, but is itself resting on the assumption. This report therefore presents
difference-in-differences as a **deflation analysis** — how much of an apparent
cross-sample effect survives removal of the reference offset — and never as a primary
result. An earlier bin-level version of this construction was **withdrawn** for violating
the assumption outright, and that is documented rather than quietly dropped.

## What n = 1 permits

One patient, two sections. Every result here is **descriptive of this case**. Confidence
intervals and q-values quantify sampling variability *across regions of this tissue*;
they say nothing about how often the finding would recur in other patients, and no
statistical procedure applied to one patient can. Statements are written as "in this
node", not "in follicular lymphoma". The two samples are the same clone from the same
person, which is what makes the internal comparison unusually clean and simultaneously
makes generalisation impossible.
